title: Allocating and releasing memory
objective: By the end of this lesson you can allocate, resize, and release heap memory correctly, and you recognise the four failure modes that account for most memory defects in C.

blocks.caption: The four functions
lines: void *calloc(size_t n, size_t size);    /* n items, zeroed, overflow-checked */
void *realloc(void *p, size_t size);    /* resize an existing block */

blocks.caption: The correct shape of an allocation
lines: int *values = malloc(count * sizeof *values);   /* sizeof *values survives a type change */
values = NULL;      /* the pointer no longer refers to anything valid */

blocks.title: Write sizeof *pointer, not sizeof(Type)
blocks.text: malloc(n * sizeof *values) keeps working when values changes from int * to long *. malloc(n * sizeof(int)) silently allocates the wrong amount the day someone changes the type — and the result is an under-allocated buffer, which is a memory-corruption bug rather than a compile error.
calloc: zeroed, and it checks the multiplication

blocks.caption: Two differences that matter
lines: int *a = malloc(n * sizeof *a);    /* contents are whatever was there before */
int *b = calloc(n, sizeof *b);     /* every byte is zero */
int *c = malloc(n * sizeof(int));  /* n * 4 may overflow and wrap to a small number */
int *d = calloc(n, sizeof(int));   /* calloc must detect the overflow and return NULL */

blocks.title: The multiplication overflow is a real attack pattern
blocks.text: If a count comes from input and you compute count * size yourself, a large count can wrap around to a small product. malloc succeeds with a tiny buffer, the code then writes count elements into it, and you have a heap overflow. calloc is required to detect that overflow — which is why it is the safer choice whenever the count is not a constant you wrote.

blocks.caption: Never assign realloc's result to the original pointer
lines: /* WRONG: if realloc fails it returns NULL and the original block is leaked */
free(buf);          /* the old block is still valid — decide deliberately */
/* realloc may move the block, so any other pointer into the old memory is now dangling. */

rows: A leak — memory grows until the process is restarted
Sanitizer or Valgrind reports it at exit
Reads or writes memory that may now belong to something else
Usually aborts immediately with an allocator message
Undefined — the allocator never owned it

blocks.title: Setting the pointer to NULL after free turns two bugs into one loud failure
blocks.text: free(p); p = NULL; costs one line. A later use-after-free then becomes a NULL dereference, which crashes immediately at the point of the mistake instead of quietly corrupting whatever now occupies that memory. And free(NULL) is explicitly a no-op, so a double free becomes harmless too.

items: Every allocation has exactly one owner, and the owner frees it
Free in the same layer that allocated, when you can — a function that allocates and returns must document who frees
Free in the reverse order of allocation when objects reference each other
On an error path, free everything acquired so far — this is what the cleanup goto is for
Never free memory you did not allocate, and never free the same block twice

blocks.title: Commit each mistake under a sanitizer
steps: Write a program that mallocs and never frees, then run it with -fsanitize=address

On Linux you get a LeakSanitizer report naming the allocation. On macOS Apple clang ships AddressSanitizer WITHOUT leak detection, so the program exits silently — verified: the same binary reports nothing on macOS and a 100-byte direct leak on Linux
If you are on macOS, use leaks -atExit -- ./prog instead, or run the exercise inside a Linux container
Write a use-after-free; run it and read where the sanitizer says the memory was freed
Write a double free; run it and read the allocator's message
Fix all three by adding free and setting the pointer to NULL
Write the realloc pattern correctly with a tmp pointer
Compare: int *a = malloc(4 * sizeof *a); versus sizeof(int) — change the type and see which one still allocates correctly
Run: valgrind ./prog     (if installed) and compare its report to the sanitizer's
blocks.expected: Three reports naming the exact allocation line, the exact free line, and the exact misuse. Those reports are why these bugs are findable in C at all — and why running tests under a sanitizer belongs in CI.

cheatsheet: malloc(n * sizeof *p) — write sizeof *p so a type change cannot break it
Always check the result for NULL
calloc(n, size) zeroes the memory and detects the multiplication overflow
Use calloc when the count comes from input — malloc's product can wrap
realloc: assign to a temporary; on NULL the original block is still yours
realloc may move the block, invalidating other pointers into it
free once, then set the pointer to NULL; free(NULL) is safe
The four failures: leak, use-after-free, double free, freeing a non-heap pointer
One owner per allocation, documented; free everything on the error path

checkpoint.prompt: Why prefer malloc(n * sizeof *values) over malloc(n * sizeof(int)) ?

choices.B: It stays correct when the pointer's type changes; the explicit type silently under-allocates the day someone edits the declaration
choices.D: It avoids the need to check for NULL

checkpoint.explanation: An under-allocated buffer is a memory-corruption bug, not a compile error, so this small habit removes a defect that is otherwise easy to introduce.

checkpoint.prompt: A count comes from user input and you write malloc(count * sizeof(int)). What is the risk?

choices.B: The multiplication can overflow and wrap to a small number, so malloc succeeds with a tiny buffer that the code then overruns
choices.C: malloc cannot take a computed size
choices.D: There is no risk if count is unsigned

checkpoint.explanation: calloc is required to detect that overflow and return NULL, which is why it is the right choice for input-derived counts.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is buf = realloc(buf, size); dangerous?

choices.B: If realloc fails it returns NULL, overwriting your only pointer to the still-valid original block — which is now leaked
choices.D: It does not preserve the contents

checkpoint.explanation: Assign to a temporary first, then decide what to do on failure while you still hold the original pointer.

checkpoint.prompt: What does setting a pointer to NULL immediately after free achieve?

choices.B: A later use becomes a NULL dereference that crashes at the mistake, and a second free becomes a harmless no-op
choices.D: It is required by the standard

checkpoint.explanation: It converts two silent, hard-to-trace bugs into one immediate and obvious failure — at the cost of a single line.
